claims.text: The target material is bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr.
The low-temperature specimen is nominally pure and defect-limited.
The high-temperature specimen contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
A feature-transformation module learned from binary-alloy data can provide expandable features for multielement alloys.
The binary-data feature transformation can be adapted to represent defects and interstitial oxygen for conductivity prediction.
Defect scattering dominates the electrical conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr from nearly 0 to 200 K.
Thermally activated processes and impurity effects are significant for oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Interstitial oxygen and other point defects cause local lattice distortions and additional scattering centers.
Oxygen and point defects modify the electronic structure relative to an ideal HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
Oxygen concentration and vacancy-density proxies can account for additional electron scattering and altered phonon interactions.
Including defect-related descriptors compensates for limitations of analytical models that assume perfect crystals.
Machine-learning models can accurately predict properties of high-entropy alloys from engineered features and experimental datasets.
The enhanced model will predict HfNbTaTiZr conductivity with less than 15% error in both specified temperature regimes.
Ideal-crystal analytical models will have more than 30% conductivity error.
Analytical calculations on ideal defect-free crystals omit conductivity reductions caused by defects and oxygen impurities.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model's temperature applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Conductivity measurements on near-stoichiometric and 1 wt.% oxygen specimens can benchmark the defect-aware model against an ideal-crystal analytical model.
Failure to obtain less than 15% error while the analytical baseline exceeds 30% error in either regime falsifies the hypothesis.
